summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for negotiating what happens when a horizontal tab character is sent to a terminal. The two sides can agree on who handles the tab, for example whether it is passed through or turned into something else. It is historic.

eli5.summary: When you press Tab on a typewriter, something has to decide how far to jump. This note lets two computers agree who decides that, and how.

subtitle: Deciding who handles horizontal tab characters in Telnet output.

tldr.problem: When a tab character is sent over Telnet, the receiving system must decide what to do with it: pass it through, replace it with spaces or a delay, or discard it. The two sides need to agree on the handling.
tldr.mechanism: The option lets the sender and receiver negotiate via Telnet commands. Each side proposes how it wants to handle tabs—ignore them, simulate them with spaces, discard them, delay after them, or wait for a response from the other direction. Values 0 to 255 encode the different strategies.
tldr.outcome: Both sides know how incoming tab characters will be processed. The RFC is Historic and no longer widely used in practice.

today: RFC 654 is Historic and no longer used in practice. Modern terminal applications typically pass tab characters through, replace them with spaces, or disable tabs entirely, without negotiation.

sections.title: The Telnet Tab Character Disposition Option
sections.content: RFC 654 defines the NAOHTD option (Negotiate About Output Horizontal Tab Disposition), a Telnet option for handling the horizontal tab character (ASCII 9) when it appears in output. Unlike RFC 653, which specifies where tabs land, this RFC specifies what happens to a tab character: whether it is sent as-is, replaced with spaces, discarded, or treated some other way. Different terminals and systems handle tabs differently, so negotiation is needed.
sections.eli5: Computers need to agree: when a Tab character arrives, what should happen—send it to the printer, turn it into spaces, skip it, or pause after it?

sections.title: Tab Disposition Strategies
sections.content:
The option defines eight strategies, encoded as values 0 to 255 in subnegotiation messages. A value of 0 means the sender will handle the tab (process it itself). Values 1 to 250 mean the receiver should handle it, with a delay (the value is the number of NUL characters to insert after the tab to slow output). Value 251 means replace the tab with a space. Value 252 means discard the tab entirely. Value 253 means simulate the tab by calculating the next tab stop and inserting spaces to reach it. Value 254 means wait for a character on the opposite connection before continuing (a flow-control technique). Value 255 means the receiver should handle it but with no specific instruction.

The key rule: if both sides want to handle tabs, the sender wins. If neither wants to, the receiver must.
sections.eli5: The option has eight choices: 0 means I will handle it; 1-250 means handle it and wait that long; 251 means turn it into a space; 252 means delete it; 253 means simulate it with spaces; 254 means wait for a reply first; 255 means you handle it your way.

sections.title: Choosing and Applying the Disposition
sections.content: The negotiation process mirrors RFC 653: both sides exchange DO, WILL, DON'T, and WON'T commands, then use subnegotiation (IAC SB) to propose a value. The sender uses code DS (1) and the receiver uses code DR (0). Once agreement is reached on a disposition, all tab characters are handled that way until one side requests a change or refuses negotiation. The RFC notes that for delay-based methods, the delay is implemented by inserting NUL bytes (null characters) immediately after the tab to slow the network transmission.
sections.eli5: Both sides negotiate using the standard Telnet commands, agree on a disposition value, and then apply it to every Tab that arrives until they negotiate again.
